prompt:
以下はある英語ニュースpodcast記事のFull Story・Point One・Point Twoです。
Point One・Point Twoそれぞれについて、以下6項目を判定してください
(それぞれPASS/FAIL)。

- qa_not_caveat_only: このPointが、研究上の限界・一般化上の注意・免責事項
  だけで構成されていない場合PASS(それらに加えて実質的な新しい内容がある
  場合もPASS。留保だけでPoint枠全体が終わっている場合はFAIL)
- qa_not_full_story_paraphrase: Full Storyの要約・言い換えに留まっていない
  場合PASS(Full Storyの中心的なlogic・結論を語彙だけ変えて繰り返している
  場合はFAIL)
- qa_not_other_point_paraphrase: もう一方のPointの要約・言い換えになって
  いない場合PASS
- qa_explains_why_it_matters: 「だから何なのか」を具体的に説明できている
  場合PASS(聞き手にとっての具体的な意味・示唆がある場合)
- qa_specific_not_generic: この記事のLedger固有の内容に基づいており、他の
  どんな記事にもほぼそのまま流用できる一般論になっていない場合PASS
- qa_adds_new_value: 新しい理解・解釈・意外性・具体的示唆のいずれかを
  実際に加えている場合PASS(Full Storyだけを聞いた場合と比べて、聞き手の
  理解が実際に深まっている場合)

reasoningには、判定理由を1〜2文の日本語で書いてください(特にFAILの場合は
具体的な理由を明記してください)。

【Full Story】
At first, a notification seems like a small event. A sound arrives. You do not touch the phone. You keep looking at the page. Yet the message can enter your thoughts before you decide to open it.

That is the puzzle behind two studies. The first, published in 2022, tested 73 college students during a long visual attention task. Researchers included phone alerts and neutral sounds in the task. The students did not look at or touch a phone. Even so, their responses were slower after the alert, and the alert required more mental control than the neutral sound.

The second study, published in 2023, looked at a different moment: before any alert arrived. Forty-two university students took an attention test with a phone on the desk or in another room. The phone was switched off, and no notifications were received. Performance was lower when the phone was on the desk.

Together, the studies suggest a two-part story. The alert can pull attention when it appears. The nearby device can also remain part of the mental scene when it is silent. The research does not show that every person reacts in exactly the same way. But it does show why “I never checked my phone” may not tell the whole story of a disrupted task.

There is also a familiar daily pattern behind these laboratory findings. In a 2018 survey of US teens aged 13 to 17, 72% said they often or sometimes checked messages or notifications before doing much else after waking. About four in ten said they felt anxious, upset, or lonely when their phone was not nearby. Most did not describe their use as an addiction, yet the report presented checking as a habit that can be hard to resist.

【Point One】
The sound experiment points to a hidden cost. A person can keep their eyes and hands away from the screen, yet still spend mental effort pushing back against an alert and finding the task again. That is different from visible phone checking: the control work happens quietly, before any screen check. Not checking is not the same as paying no cognitive cost.

【Point Two】
A silent phone is not the same as a distant phone. In the study of 42 university students, the phone was off and no notifications arrived. Yet both attention and speed scores were lower when it sat on the desk than when it was in another room. For deep work, distance may remove a background readiness that silence leaves behind.

point_one.reasoning: 通知を見ていなくても、注意を戻すための認知的コストが発生するという「見えない負担」を明確にし、目に見えるスマホ確認とは異なる意味を示している。Full Storyの実験結果を踏まえつつ、「確認しなかったから無影響」とは言えないという具体的な理解を加えている。

point_two.reasoning: 電源が切れていても、机上にあること自体が深い作業を妨げうるという、沈黙と距離の違いを具体化している。研究結果を「集中が必要な作業では別室に置く」という実践的な示唆へつなげており、Point Oneの通知音の問題とも重ならない。
